nodes.name: NiCP-NS Co-precipitation
nodes.procedure: sodium citrate (4 mmol) and K₂Ni(CN)₄·nH₂O (4 mmol) were dissolved into water (20 mL) to obtain a clear solution. Then nickel acetate tetrahydrate (4 mmol) was added into another 20 mL of water. The two solutions were then sufficiently mixed and kept stationary state for complete reaction at room temperature for 24 h. The obtained blue product was then centrifuged and washed several times with distilled water and absolute ethanol and subsequently dried in a vacuum oven at 70°C for 24 h for further use.

nodes.name: Fe-NiCP-NS Co-precipitation
nodes.procedure: For the preparation of Fe-NiCP-NS, ferrous chloride (2 at%) was used instead of nickel acetate tetrahydrate following the same procedure: sodium citrate (4 mmol) and K₂Ni(CN)₄·nH₂O (4 mmol) were dissolved into water (20 mL) to obtain a clear solution. Then ferrous chloride (2 at%) was added into another 20 mL of water. The two solutions were then sufficiently mixed and kept stationary state for complete reaction at room temperature for 24 h. The obtained blue product was then centrifuged and washed several times with distilled water and absolute ethanol and subsequently dried in a vacuum oven at 70°C for 24 h for further use.

nodes.source_text: Long-term stability is an important property of the HER catalyst. It is observed that the Fe-Ni₃C-2% electrocatalyst remains stable with negligible degradation in the alkaline solutions after 1000th cycles

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD patterns confirm formation of Ni3C structure (JCPDS card no. 19-2869) without detectable impurity phase for all Ni3C samples.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After carburization, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of all Ni3C samples acquired (Supporting Information, Figure S3), which confirms the formation of the Ni3C structure (JCPDS card no. 19-2869) without a detectable impurity phase.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM shows uniform 2D nanosheet structures with lateral size of 200-300 nm and thickness of 10 nm for both Ni3C and Fe-Ni3C-2% samples.
nodes.evidence_snippet: It is clear that the sample retains the uniform two dimensional (2D) structures and is composed of numerous overlapped nanosheets with the lateral size of about 200-300 nm and the thickness of about 10 nm (Figure 1a).

properties.features: High-resolution imaging showing nanostructure and morphology

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM reveals uniform 3-5 nm Ni3C nanodots embedded in amorphous carbon for Ni3C nanosheets; Fe-Ni3C-2% shows lattice fringes of 0.202 nm corresponding to (113) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The TEM images of the Ni3C nanosheets clearly show numerous crystalline Ni3C nanodots (about 3-5 nm), and amorphous carbon was generated through the pyrolysis of NiCP precursors.

properties.description: High-resolution image showing nanoparticles with lattice fringes

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM of Fe-Ni3C-2% shows lattice spacing of 0.202 nm corresponding to the (113) planes.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The observed lattice fringes in the HRTEM image (Figure 1f) show the spacing of 0.202 nm, corresponding to the distance of the (113) planes of Fe-Ni3C-2%.

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM-EDS reveals homogeneous distribution of Ni, C, and N elements in Ni3C nanosheets and Fe, Ni, C, N in Fe-Ni3C-2%.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The HAADF-STEM image (Supporting Information, Figure S4) reveals that the Ni3C nanosheets are indeed composed of Ni, C, and N elements, which are homogenously distributed in a nanosheet.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS of Fe-Ni3C-2% shows Ni 2p3/2 peak at 855.4 eV corresponding to Ni3C phase, satellite at 861.6 eV, Fe 2p3 peaks at 704.7 eV and 710.1 eV indicating Fe doping, N 1s peaks at 396.9 eV (C=N, pyridine-like N) and 399 eV (C-N, graphite-like N), and C 1s peaks including sp3-hybridized C at 284.3 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to study the valence states and bonding structures of Fe-Ni3C-2% nanosheets (Figure 2a). In the Ni2p3/2 XPS spectrum (Figure 2b), a peak with a binding energy of 855.4 eV and a satellite peak at 861.6 eV were observed. The main peak position located at 855.4 eV corresponds to the Ni3C phase. The XPS Fe 2p3 spectrum (Figure 2c) shows binding energies at around 704.7 and 710.1 eV, indicating the doping of Fe in Ni3C. The N 1s peak shown in Figure 2d corresponds to nitrogen atoms in C=N bonds (396.9 eV) and C-N bonds (399 eV).

nodes.characterization_summary: BET specific surface area of Fe-Ni3C-2% is 151.2 m2/g with pore size of 4-8 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The BET specific surface area is calculated to be 151.2 m2 g-1 based on the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherm plot with the pore size of 4-8 nm (Supporting Information, Figure S7).

nodes.characterization_summary: EIS shows smaller semicircular diameter (charge transfer resistance) for Fe-Ni3C-2% compared to Ni3C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Besides, the semicircular diameter in the electrochemical impedance spectrum (EIS) of Fe-Ni3C-2% is much smaller than that of Ni3C, which indicates smaller charge transfer resistance in Fe-Ni3C-2% (Supporting Information, Figure S13).

nodes.characterization_summary: CV used for electroactivation (100 mV/s for 20 cycles) and to measure double layer capacitance Cdl = 6.8 mF/cm² for Fe-Ni3C-2%, largest among samples indicating highest electrochemically active surface area.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To improve the OER performance, all three catalysts were pretreated with cyclic voltammetry (CV) at 100 mV s-1 for 20 scan cycles as electroactivation. ... electrochemical double layer capacitance (Cdl) was used to evaluate the electrochemically active surface area ... Fe-Ni3C-2% catalyst exhibits the largest Cdl (6.8 mF cm-2) among all three samples.
